newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean won seen troubled until mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: South Korean won seen troubled until mid-1997.

text.p: The troubled South Korean won, hovering at six-year lows, is expected to sink further until mid-1997 when the country's key exports begin a long-awaited recovery, analysts said on Wednesday.

The won, down seven percent since January, is considered a casualty of one of South Korea's most troubling economic ills -- a fast-deteriorating current account deficit that has swung wide open with a plunge in exports of key locally produced goods.

The trend over the next six months looks much the same, the analysts said. Prices for two of the nation's major exports, computer chips and petrochemicals, continue to struggle on global markets with a recovery not expected until early 1997.
Most see the won, which surged in 1995 with an explosion in exports, retreating further in the next six months as local firms seek more U.S. dollars to finance a rising import bill.
Strength in the dollar, particularly against the Japanese yen, has only added to the local currency's misery.
"The strong dollar in international markets is a factor that will retain the weak won," said Chang Sun Lee, analyst at the LG Economic Research Institute in Seoul.
The analysts said the won's slide partly reflected a desire in the government under new Finance Minister Han Seung-soo for a cheaper currency to help revive exports.
"There's no coincidence that the won began depreciating soon after the finance minister took office," said Steve Marvin, economist at Ssangyong Investment and Securities.

Han took over the finance ministry in August, when the won had been trading in a relatively tight range of 813-814. By mid-August, it was tumbling fast, hitting its weakest level in six years on August 16 at 826.
Selling gathered steam in September as the current account deficit ballooned to $15 billion, with economists projecting a staggering $20 billion deficit for all of 1996.
The won hit a fresh six-year low on October 9, trading at 830.30 to the dollar, prompting a vigorous defence by the central bank which supported the unit by selling dollars.

Economists describe the Bank of Korea's intervention as only a temporary measure to smooth the won's decline and prevent any jump in import prices, which in turn could threaten the economy with an inflationary backlash.
On Wednesday, the won was trading at 828 to the dollar.

Despite the intervention, analysts said Han, whose predecessor lost his job because of the deficit crisis, appeared intent on cutting the deficit with the help of a weaker currency, delivering exporters a gift by effectively lowering the price of Korean goods sold abroad.

Most expect the rot in the won to stop around the middle of next year when prices for those goods begin to rise in tandem with strength in the global economy, a situation which is expected to help repair the deficit.
"I assume that when the trade account stabilises, the government will stop this ill-conceived action of allowing the won to slide," said Marvin at Ssangyong.
He said the won had the potential to weaken further to 840-850 by the end of 1996 and then begin a recovery next year to finish 1997 at around 800.
Another interbank dealer at a foreign investment firm forecast a similar range, tipping a further slide to 860-870 by the end of 1996 and then a recovery to 815 by the end of 1997.
